title: Why cats purr
text: The purr is the cat's most {{1}} noise: it happens on both the in-breath and the out-breath, without pauses, at roughly twenty-five to thirty vibrations a second. How cats manage it took science until 2023 to {{2}}: pads of tissue in the larynx turn out to be {{3}} of purring at exactly that frequency with no conscious effort at all — the cat simply breathes, and the machinery hums. The more {{4}} question is why. Purring is not only happiness: cats purr while nursing, while injured, at the vet, and in the hours before dying, leading researchers to describe it as a {{5}} signal — self-soothing, a request to stay near, or both. There is even a {{6}} case for healing: the dominant frequencies sit in a range that has been {{7}} with improved bone density in other mammals, and one explanation offered for why cats' bones heal so well is that they {{8}} themselves with ultrasound several hours a day. The house cat, in other words, may spend its afternoons running physiotherapy on its own skeleton, and call it a nap.

gaps.explanation: 'the cat's most mysterious noise' — long unexplained; meticulous = extremely careful.
'took science until 2023 to unravel' — untangle the mechanism; unveil = reveal formally.
'tissue capable of purring at that frequency' — 'capable of' is the fixed pattern; capricious = unpredictable.
'the more perplexing question is why' — the puzzling one; perpetuate = keep something going.
'a flexible signal — self-soothing, a request, or both' — adaptable in function; flimsy = weakly made.
'a plausible case for healing' — believable on the evidence; pliable = easily bent.
'frequencies associated with improved bone density' — found alongside it; assimilate = absorb into a group.
'they bathe themselves with ultrasound' — soak in it, figuratively; baste = moisten meat while cooking.
